title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
description: Image source, BBC/James WatkinsByPaul Glynn & Mark SavageFast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursd
body: Image source, BBC/James WatkinsByPaul Glynn & Mark SavageFast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.Figure caption, Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.But after three more gigs this weekend and one added one next, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her."Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me."I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."'Big shoes to fill'Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC."The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted."No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill."But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."Next month she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked"."'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request."It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zane were my favourites."So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

schema.headline: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run

title: Can Andy Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?
description: Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.He saw how last year's welfare r
body: Andy Burnham has committed to bringing the welfare bill down, but he knows just how the high the political stakes are.He saw how last year's welfare rebellion marked the beginning of the end for his predecessor in Downing Street.Sir Keir Starmer's authority was shredded when 120 - more than a quarter - of his own MPs threatened to derail his reforms.To defuse this, Sir Keir was compelled to guarantee that existing claimants of personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales, wouldn't lose out.Even then, 49 of the 120 potential Labour rebels still voted against their own government.Next week, a review from former New Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn has the capacity to create another internal row in Labour's ranks.  Milburn has spent a year grappling with how to reduce the nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).In an interview with the Times, he has now confirmed he is set to recommend cutting benefits for some 16-24 year olds who currently receive Pip, or the enhanced health-related payment of Universal Credit.Taking benefit cuts to the Parliamentary Labour Party would usually have a similar effect to adding phosphorous to water.But from my soundings, the deep waters of the Labour ranks are calmer than might be expected.Why? Importantly, two of the most effective organisers of last year's welfare rebellion are batting for the current prime minister, rather than against the previous one. Louise Haigh is now the most powerful cabinet minister after Andy Burnham himself, while Anneliese Midgeley is his chief whip. And the MP who fronted that rebellion - Meg Hillier - has said she wants to give Milburn's proposals a "fair wind".There are also clear differences to the previous approach to welfare reform. First, it is not being presented as primarily a cost-cutting exercise with pre-determined savings. Instead, there will be upfront investment to provide more support to unemployed young people, and a timeframe for net savings likely to be set at around a decade – gradualism, not a short, sharp shock.Second, last year's initial reforms would have affected people in all age groups, whilst benefit cuts this time would be limited to the under 25s, who make up around 11% of Pip claimants.I've spoken to government ministers who had expressed concerns – at least privately – about the changes devised previously by Rachel Reeves and Liz Kendall.  This time, they are on board.One of them told me that so long as there was enough support for young people, with guaranteed jobs and training, MPs would be "fine" with some benefit cuts.But they added that it was vital that those who really couldn't work wouldn't be worse off. Milburn will suggest there could even be enhanced payments for people in this category, while some young people with disabilities who lose out on Pip could nonetheless be given an additional "allowance" to help with living costs.Another minister who opposed the previous reforms praised the process this time. There had been a high level of engagement not just from Milburn, but Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, who has been taking MPs through the principles behind the reforms.One minister was a little more cautious, suggesting support for a reduction in benefits would depend on what the entire "package" of reforms looked like. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be wide-ranging – from pre-school policies to how the NHS deals with mental health.Some of the eventual 49 rebels from last year are in a similar place. York MP Rachael Maskell told me it was essential that she saw the detail of the proposals rather than the "drip, drip" of press reports which would "cause young people stress and distress".She felt withdrawing Pip from young people was "like a sledgehammer to crack a nut" and was concerned that some disabled people required it to remain in work. She also suggested that the government "shouldn't just point the finger at young people," and should look closely at how employers could take more youngsters on.Stroud MP Simon Opher also voted against the government on welfare last year. He told me there was a "crisis" with so many Neets, and Milburn had come up with a "credible solution".But he believes cutting benefits should be a "last resort" and is worried about restricting access to the health element of Universal Credit, as a quarter of young claimants aren't Neet. He concludes that the "devil will be in the detail".So much of politics - like comedy – depends on timing.For some sceptics, including serving ministers, the Milburn proposals will be more warmly welcomed if support for young people is in place before entitlements are withdrawn.But for some Labour MPs, cutting payments to existing claimants crosses a line.Clapham and Brixton Hill MP Bell Ribiero-Addy has she wasn't sure she could back cuts.Referring to Pip, she didn't believe that "you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work".And another MP on the left of the party, Brian Leishman, told the BBC he couldn't back benefits cuts as "we are in the middle of a cost of living crisis".So a welfare rebellion seems guaranteed if Burnham accepts Milburn's recommendations.But it seems unlikely to be of the same scale, or have a similar level of political jeopardy to the one which shook the Starmer government.

schema.headline: Can Andy Burnham avoid another Labour welfare rebellion?

title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
description: Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next ro
body: Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union. On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table". "He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war."Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

schema.headline: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks

title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
description: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.Uk
body: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic. Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details."The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace. He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

schema.headline: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland

title: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
description: If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me.The man who co-founded this enormously
body: If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me.The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life.It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future. It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague, or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper. Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build.This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response. But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery. The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula. In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side.But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far. His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up.Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd. During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated). He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie.Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles. The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering. I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it.For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him. He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long.Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings. Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career.Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia.She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive.But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical. She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang.A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms.As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next. He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang. And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations. It's a painfully personal matter.

schema.headline: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions

title: Andy Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
description: Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought the
body: Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.  Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line."But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration". Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

schema.headline: Andy Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU

title: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
description: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.A video of a Veterans Day
body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet. In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads. In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

schema.headline: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group

title: Junior doctor burnout may put maternity patients at risk, regulator warns
description: Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is wa
body: Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.It found:Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialtiesThey were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialtiesOne in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of traineesCharlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients."Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby."I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago."The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing."There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry."It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world."Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."The main challenge, she says, are the sheer number of demands placed on a doctor in her field."It could be that there's two or three ladies whose babies need delivering, and then somebody else coming in on maternity triage whose baby isn't moving, and you might also be getting calls from A&E about a lady having a miscarriage who's bleeding really heavily."There's just one of you to manage all those jobs."Broughton says while she has largely had positive experiences, it is important to step back and look at the wider culture."You do hear things from other hospitals about people feeling nervous about calling the consultant...which isn't great."Dr Kat Barton, chair of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) National Trainee Committee, says workplace issues end up affecting patients."Many of us feel overstretched and close to burnout. This reflects staff shortages, working beyond our hours, and knowing that despite our best efforts, the care women receive is being affected."We know the safest care comes from teams that are well-supported, well-resourced, and listen to each other and to women and families."We need the government to invest in safe staffing at every level, protect our time for training, and support our wellbeing and careers, so we can give women the safe, compassionate care they deserve."Recent high profile maternity reviews, which looked at outcomes for mothers and babies, also highlighted concerns about workplace culture, leadership and the ability of staff to raise concerns.Obstetrics and gynaecology trainees were more positive than average about some aspects of patient safety reporting, the GMC survey indicated, including how to report patient safety incidents and near misses.A DHSC spokesperson said: "In all the investigations carried out in recent years into failings in maternity services, one of the key lessons has been that members of staff must feel empowered to speak up if they have concerns about workload, or patient safety, and their concerns must be acted upon."All NHS trusts are now required to have a dedicated Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and internal pathways for staff to raise concerns about the working environment, patient safety, or their own wellbeing. "Alongside this, we are continuing to grow and strengthen the workforce to help relieve the pressures on busy maternity units, and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year."Since coming into the role in July, the Secretary of State has made maternity services a personal priority, and the Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing is working to respond to the concerns raised by staff and families alike, and ensure that every maternity unit meets the highest standards of patient safety and care."

schema.headline: Junior doctor burnout may put maternity patients at risk, regulator warns

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
description: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of be
body: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee."Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X."The American people deserve answers," he added.Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

schema.headline: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy

title: Cole Palmer: Morgan Rogers says Chelsea team-mate committed to England
description: Morgan Rogers says any suggestion Cole Palmer is not committed to England "is a lie" and "nonsense".Rogers scored the opener in Wednesday's 2-1 Uefa N
body: Morgan Rogers says any suggestion Cole Palmer is not committed to England "is a lie" and "nonsense".Rogers scored the opener in Wednesday's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Croatia, with Harry Kane adding a penalty on his record-breaking 126th appearance for the men's side.But his Chelsea team-mate, and childhood friend, Palmer had been left out of the squad after boss Thomas Tuchel said he "misses too many chances to impress".The 24-year-old Palmer, who was also not called up for the World Cup, withdrew from the previous England camp in September citing a minor injury.Forward Rogers, also 24, was asked about the criticism of Palmer following the win at Wembley, and told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He wants to be here. "He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done. "He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn't feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself. "But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 or 15 years, he also has to manage himself. If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it. "It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It's a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. It's a lie."You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don't get it and he doesn't get it."In the three years since his England debut, Palmer has only won 14 caps, scoring two goals - including one in the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain - and having one assist.That is despite scoring 50 Premier League goals with 24 assists.He was named England's men's player of the year for the 2023-24 season after some impressive form, including his strike against Spain in the Berlin showpiece.But Palmer has only featured in three of Tuchel's 27 games since he succeeded Gareth Southgate as manager.Some sketchy form last season, though, meant the former Manchester City player missed out on the the summer World Cup, with England going on to finish third after losing to Argentina in the semi-final.He was named in Tuchel's first squad after that, but withdrew despite having played in all Chelsea's league games to that point.Tuchel said this week: "We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together."I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception."We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."But the German added: "It's not personal. We will never assume Cole is in the mindset never to come to the camp."Cole is always in our mindset but the competition is on."

schema.headline: Cole Palmer: Morgan Rogers says Chelsea team-mate committed to England

title: Ankle injuries are more common than you think - here's how to protect yours
description: Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles. "A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps,
body: Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles. "A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front."It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over?"Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular  - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them."She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task. She says different activities require different shoes. "If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place."Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate."For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree."

schema.headline: Ankle injuries are more common than you think - here's how to protect yours

title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
description: Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property l
body: Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r)ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsHave you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place. But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing". So how much AI enhancement is too much? 'The rooms were much smaller'Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place. "The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, AI has been used to make the property look more luxuriousIt later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI. But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time. "It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for." All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down. 'A surge of AI listings'Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible. It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly. According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential. But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time. "I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person." He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.Image source, Howards/SuppliedImage caption, Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove. In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter. In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing. "If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.Image source, Howards/SuppliedImage caption, In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug  A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property". "It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."'Jumping on the bandwagon'Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology. But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing. He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.  "My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."Additional reporting by Star McFarlane

schema.headline: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?

title: Jack Grealish issues Everton apology following disciplinary breach
description: Jack Grealish has issued an apology to Everton fans for his recent absence due to a disciplinary issue.The on-loan Manchester City midfielder missed t
body: Jack Grealish has issued an apology to Everton fans for his recent absence due to a disciplinary issue.The on-loan Manchester City midfielder missed the Toffees' two games against Newcastle United in the Premier League and Carabao Cup, as well as the win against Coventry prior to the international break, following a "breach of club discipline".But he returned to action for the first time on Thursday, featuring in a behind-closed-doors victory against Championship side Derby County.The 31-year-old posted an apology to the club and fans social media, saying he "can't wait to be back playing in front of you.""Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a good few days training," Grealish wrote on his Instagram story."I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks. "I love playing for this club and can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt. See you soon."Before Everton's game against Coventry, manager David Moyes was asked if the international break would give Everton the opportunity to resolve the issue with Grealish, to which he said: "We just need to wait and see how things go." Grealish is trying to rebuild his career at Everton, having fallen out of favour at City despite costing the club £100m in 2021.He scored twice in 22 games for Everton last season during a loan spell which was cut short by injury.The midfielder returned to the club for a second loan spell this season but had only made six appearances before falling out of favour.

schema.headline: Jack Grealish issues Everton apology following disciplinary breach

title: Man Utd's Mauricio Pochettino pursuit and Michael Carrick decisions
description: Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who
body: Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.United liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis. The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.United are third bottom of the Premier League and 17th in the Champions League table.

schema.headline: Man Utd's Mauricio Pochettino pursuit and Michael Carrick decisions

title: Planning permission granted for MoD Bicester asylum centre plans
description: Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.Th
body: Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: "Over 1,200 unvetted illegal migrant men are being dumped in Piddington."Tory and Labour governments have betrayed their own people. Reform will detain and deport all of these men."A Home Office spokesperson said: "A final decision to proceed is yet to be taken."The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election."This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. "These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community."The government must house asylum seekers - people who want to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence - if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered.Labour has pledged to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels by 2029, an expensive form of accommodation which have become a focal point for anti-migrant protests in parts of the country. Ministers are looking for large, alternative sites - including former military bases - where they can be housed instead.Home Office data showed that the number of asylum applications dropped 21% in the year to June 2026, at 85,891.

schema.headline: Planning permission granted for MoD Bicester asylum centre plans
